items.passage: Education is often described as the pursuit of knowledge, yet much of modern education is better described as the pursuit of credentials. A degree is not only, and sometimes not mainly, a record of what a student has learned. It is a signal, a way for an employer to sort a pile of applications quickly, to distinguish those who have passed a filter from those who have not. The signal works only as long as it is scarce. When everyone holds a degree, the degree alone no longer distinguishes anyone, and students must collect further credentials, a master's, a certificate, an internship, to stand out. The result is a race in which each generation must run further to reach the same place, spending more years and more money on signals that convey less information than they once did. This does not mean learning is worthless. It means the system rewards the appearance of learning more reliably than learning itself, and students, responding rationally to the incentives, optimise for grades and certificates rather than for understanding. A student who spends a term wrestling with a difficult idea may learn more than one who memorises the textbook, yet the second student will often receive the better grade. The remedy is not to abolish credentials, which serve a real purpose in sorting large numbers of applicants, but to separate the signal from the learning. Employers could test skills directly, universities could assess understanding rather than recall, and students could be judged by what they can do rather than by the certificates they hold. Until that separation happens, education will continue to produce graduates who are well credentialed and poorly educated, and the race for signals will continue to consume years that might have been spent learning. Employers contribute to the race when they raise degree requirements for jobs that do not need them, asking for a master's degree for work that could be learned in weeks. That practice, sometimes called credential inflation, forces applicants to spend years acquiring qualifications that add little to their ability to do the job, while excluding capable people who cannot afford the time or money. The employer gains a simple filter, and loses a wider pool of talent, yet the cost is borne by the applicant, not by the employer, so the practice continues. A fairer approach would be to test for the skills the job actually requires, and to value experience, portfolios and practical demonstrations as highly as certificates, so that the signal is tied to the work itself rather than to the length of time a person spent in a classroom.

items.passage: A city can be crowded and lonely at the same time. Millions of people may live within a few square miles, sharing buses, lifts and pavements, yet never speak to one another, never learn a neighbour's name, never feel that they belong to the place where they live. Loneliness, in this account, is not the absence of people. It is the absence of belonging, the feeling that one is surrounded by strangers who will not notice if one disappears. Urban life is particularly good at producing this feeling, because it offers contact without connection. A person may interact with dozens of people in a day, a shopkeeper, a driver, a colleague, without any of those interactions becoming a relationship. The interactions are brief, transactional and replaceable, and they leave the person feeling more alone than if she had met no one at all. The remedy often proposed is more socialising, more events, more opportunities to meet people. Yet the problem is not a shortage of opportunities to meet strangers, but a shortage of structures that turn strangers into neighbours. A community is not a collection of individuals who happen to live near each other. It is a set of shared routines, obligations and stories, a market where the same faces return, a park where children play together, a building where people know who is ill and who needs help. Without those structures, a city is a collection of private lives lived in public, and loneliness, however crowded the streets, will persist. Housing design plays a part, because a building with no shared spaces, no courtyard and no place to linger will produce neighbours who never meet, however many people live in it. A building with a shared garden, a common room and a staircase wide enough for conversation will produce, over time, a community, not because its residents are friendlier but because its design gives them reasons to encounter each other. Urban planners who understand this design for encounter, placing benches where people wait, markets where they shop, and parks where children play, so that the city itself becomes a structure for belonging. A city built only for movement, for cars and for speed, will move people efficiently and leave them lonely, because it has designed out the very encounters that turn strangers into neighbours.

items.passage: History is often imagined as a record of what happened, but collective memory is something different. It is the story a group tells itself about its past, shaped as much by what it chooses to forget as by what it chooses to remember. A nation may remember its victories in detail and its crimes in vague outline, not because the crimes did not happen but because remembering them would disturb the story it tells about itself. Forgetting, in this account, is not an accident. It is a choice, made collectively and often unconsciously, to preserve a particular identity. The difficulty is that forgetting does not erase the past. It merely postpones the reckoning, and the past, unremembered, returns in other forms: in resentment, in distrust, in the repetition of old mistakes by people who do not know they are repeating them. A society that remembers honestly is not one that remembers everything, since no society can, but one that remembers the difficult parts as well as the proud ones, and that allows different groups within it to remember differently without accusing each other of disloyalty. Memory, in this sense, is not a luxury for historians. It is the material from which identity is made, and a society that cannot remember its own past cannot understand its present, or choose its future with any clarity. Museums and memorials are the places where this choice is made visible, because they decide which objects to display, which stories to tell, and which silences to preserve. A museum that displays only the triumphs of a nation tells a different story from one that displays its failures as well, and visitors who see only triumphs may leave with a pride that is unearned, while visitors who see failures may leave with a humility that is necessary. The best museums do not pretend to be neutral, because no display is neutral, but they are honest about their choices, labelling what is contested, presenting more than one perspective, and allowing visitors to form their own judgement. That honesty is itself a form of memory, a recognition that the past is not a single story but a set of stories that must be held together, even when they disagree.

items.passage: Technology is often praised for making work easier, yet ease can be a form of loss. When a machine takes over the skilled part of a job, the worker who remains may be faster, more productive and less skilled than before. A weaver who once chose threads, judged tension and repaired mistakes becomes an operator who presses a button when a light turns green. A driver who once navigated by memory and judgement becomes a follower of instructions from a screen. The work is done more quickly, but the worker knows less about how it is done, and that loss matters. Skill is not only a means to a wage. It is a source of pride, of identity, of the ability to judge whether work has been done well. A worker who has lost skill has also lost the capacity to notice when something is wrong, to improvise when the machine fails, and to teach the next generation what the work requires. The danger is not that machines will replace all workers, but that they will replace the skilled part of work, leaving workers who are dependent on systems they do not understand. A society that values only speed and output may not notice the loss until the machine breaks, and no one remembers how to do the work by hand. The remedy is not to reject technology, but to design it so that it augments skill rather than replacing it, keeping the human judgement at the centre of the work, even when the machine does the heavy lifting. Apprenticeship is the traditional answer to this problem, because it keeps the learner beside the skilled worker, watching, imitating and gradually taking on more of the task. The apprentice learns not only the movements but the judgements, when a thread is too tight, when a joint is weak, when a machine sounds wrong, and those judgements cannot be learned from a manual alone. Modern workplaces that replace apprenticeship with short training courses may produce workers who can operate a machine but cannot diagnose it, and the loss becomes visible only when the machine fails and no one knows why. Restoring apprenticeship, in new forms for new industries, would keep human judgement at the centre of work, and would ensure that skill is passed on, not merely used up, by each generation of workers.

items.passage: Justice is usually imagined as punishment. A crime is committed, a penalty is imposed, and the balance is restored. Yet punishment, however necessary, answers only one question: what does the offender deserve? It does not ask what was harmed, what would repair the harm, or what the victim needs to feel safe again. Restorative justice begins with those questions. It brings victim, offender and community together, not to decide a penalty but to agree on a repair: an apology, restitution, community service, a change in behaviour. The offender is asked not only to suffer a consequence but to understand the harm and take responsibility for repairing it. Critics argue that restorative justice is soft, that it lets offenders off lightly and fails to deter others. There is force in the worry, and restorative justice is not appropriate for every crime. But the evidence, where it has been tried carefully, suggests that victims who participate often feel more satisfied than those who go through a conventional trial, and offenders who take part are less likely to reoffend than those who simply serve a sentence. The point is not to replace punishment entirely, but to recognise that punishment alone leaves the harm unrepaired. A society that punishes without repairing may feel that justice has been done, while the victim still lives with the loss and the offender still does not understand what was done. Justice, in this account, is not only about what the offender deserves. It is about what the community needs to heal, and that healing requires more than a penalty. Youth justice is a place where the restorative approach is often tried first, because young offenders are seen as capable of change, and because the harm they cause is often reparable. A teenager who has damaged property may be asked to repair it, to meet the owner, to understand the effect of the act, and to agree on a way to make amends. That process is slower than a fine or a short sentence, and it requires the victim to be willing to participate, yet when it works, it produces something a penalty cannot, which is an offender who understands what was done and a victim who feels heard. The approach is not suitable for every case, and it should not be romanticised, but its success with young people suggests that the questions it asks, what was harmed and what would repair it, are questions that justice should ask more often, for offenders of every age.

items.explanation: Statement I follows directly: the librarians feared fewer books would come back, and the passage states that the total number of books returned each month rose by a fifth. Statement II follows directly: the passage states that the council measured success by the number of lapsed borrowers who rejoined. Statement III contradicts the passage: the council's stated measure was lapsed borrowers rejoining, and its reports recorded that more than two hundred former borrowers had taken out a book again, so nothing supports calling the change a failure on the council's measure, and the passage never mentions fine revenue as a measure at all.
options: I only
II only
I and III only
II and III only
I and II only
items.passage: When the town library stopped charging late fees, the change was welcomed by some and doubted by others. The librarians had feared that without fines, borrowers would keep books longer and fewer books would come back. In the year after the change, the total number of books returned each month rose by a fifth, and the number of borrowers visiting each week rose as well. The borrowers said the change made them less afraid to borrow, and several said they now returned books promptly because they no longer felt punished for being a day late. The council, which had introduced the change to bring lapsed borrowers back, measured its success by the number of lapsed borrowers who rejoined, and its reports recorded that more than two hundred former borrowers had taken out a book again.
items.question: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would agree with which of the following? Consider the statements below. I. The librarians' fear that ending late fees would reduce returns proved unfounded, since the total number of books returned each month rose. II. The council judged the change by whether lapsed borrowers returned to the library. III. The council regarded the change as a failure because fewer fines were collected. Select the option that lists all and only the statements the author would agree with.
items.stream_verdict: OLD: RC inference with an unsupported verdict: Statement I claimed shopkeepers regarded the ban as a success, which the passage never establishes. NEW: RC inference on a fresh passage (library late fees) where every statement is decidable from the text: I and II are directly stated, III contradicts the stated measure. COLD-SOLVE: Cold solve: I is stated (fear vs rose by a fifth), II is stated (council's measure), III contradicts the stated measure and the reported result. Unique key E (after option-order balancing).

items.explanation: The 2015 leader fell to third place by 2025, so at least two districts that started below it ended above it, and each of those must have gained more than the leader gained over the same period, which makes option D necessary. Option A is not forced, since the leader could have had the second smallest rise. Option B is not forced, since another district, such as the one that moved from fourth to first, could have gained more than the last placed district. Option C is not forced, since the district third in 2025 could be the old leader with a small rise. Option E contradicts the rank changes.
options: The district that ranked first in 2015 had the smallest increase of any district.
The district that ranked last in 2015 had the largest increase of any district.
The district that ranked third in 2025 had the largest increase of any district.
At least one district other than the 2015 leader saw its share rise by more than the 2015 leader's rise.
Every district's share rose by the same amount.

In every district the share rose, but the district that ranked first in 2015 ranked third in 2025, and the district that ranked last in 2015 ranked second in 2025. items.explanation: Recall and notification both rest on the same judgement: the batch is unsafe. The correct option establishes that in two ways: the supplier's past falsification destroys the assurance that the test was an error, and an independent retest confirms the impurity, which is exactly the reason to believe the drug is unsafe that triggers the 48-hour duty. The other options cite a cost, a dependence, or a question the doctors have asked, none of which proves the batch is unsafe.
options: The supplier has falsified quality records for this ingredient in the past, and the firm's own retest has now confirmed the impurity in a second batch.
The supplier has falsified quality records for this ingredient in the past, and a recall would cost 15 crore rupees.
The firm has no alternative supplier for this ingredient, and the drug is used to treat a common illness.
A rival firm also buys the same ingredient from this supplier, and the supplier is the cheapest source in the country.
The doctors who prescribe the drug have asked whether the packs are safe, and the firm has not yet answered them.
items.passage: A pharmaceutical firm has discovered that a key ingredient supplied for its best-selling blood pressure drug may be contaminated, after a routine test showed an impurity above the permitted limit. The firm has already distributed 20 lakh packs of the drug to pharmacies across the country, and the supplier, which provides 80 percent of the firm's supply of this ingredient, says the test result was a laboratory error and that the ingredient is safe. The firm's own quality head wants an immediate recall of all packs made with the suspect ingredient, arguing that a contaminated blood pressure drug could harm patients who depend on it daily. The commercial head warns that a recall would cost 15 crore rupees, would create a shortage of the drug for patients who need it, and would damage the firm's reputation with doctors. The regulatory affairs head notes that the regulator must be informed within 48 hours if the firm has reason to believe a drug is unsafe, and that hiding the result could lead to a factory closure. The chief executive must decide today, because the next batch of the drug is due to leave the factory tomorrow morning. The pharmacies have already sold most of the 20 lakh packs to patients who take the drug every day for blood pressure. The doctors who prescribe the drug have asked the firm whether the packs they prescribed are safe, and the firm has not yet answered them. The next batch of the drug is due to leave the factory tomorrow morning, and the production team is waiting for the chief executive's decision. The supplier provides 80 percent of the firm's supply of this ingredient and has no alternative source in the country.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support recalling the drug immediately AND informing the regulator within 48 hours?
items.stream_verdict: REBUILD: Single-step matching: option E is the direct credibility evidence against the supplier; the other options are irrelevant.

items.explanation: Twenty lakh packs have already been distributed and sold to patients. In the 48 hours of waiting, a further 2 lakh packs will be sold, so the total reaching patients is 20 lakh plus 2 lakh, which is 22 lakh packs. The 20 lakh option counts only the packs already sold and ignores the packs that will be sold while the firm waits.
options: 20 lakh packs
18 lakh packs
22 lakh packs
2 lakh packs
35 lakh packs
items.question: A day later, the quality head reports that 20 lakh packs have already been distributed, and pharmacies have sold most of them to patients who take the drug every day. A recall would cost 15 crore rupees. The firm estimates that if it waits for a second test, which takes 48 hours, a further 2 lakh packs will be sold in that time. If the drug is in fact contaminated, how many packs in total will have reached patients by the time the second test result arrives?

items.explanation: The rule must do two things: hold every suspect batch until a second, independent test clears it, and inform the regulator within 48 hours. Only the fourth option does both. The last option holds the batch but tells the regulator only after the second test, so it fails the second condition. Believing the supplier repeats the error, shipping whatever the result puts patients at risk, and delaying the regulator destroys trust.
options: The firm will always believe the supplier when the supplier says a test result was a laboratory error
The next batch will leave the factory tomorrow morning, whatever the test result, so that patients never face a shortage
The regulator will be told only after the second test, so that the firm is never seen to have doubted its supplier
No batch made with an ingredient that has failed a routine test may leave the factory until a second, independent test clears it, and the regulator must be informed within 48 hours

No batch made with an ingredient that has failed a routine test may leave the factory until a second, independent test clears it, but the regulator will be told only after the second test, so that the firm is never seen to have doubted its supplier

The board now asks for a rule that will stop a suspect ingredient from ever again being used while a test result is disputed. Which rule does BOTH things: it stops any batch made with an ingredient that has failed a routine test from leaving the factory until a second, independent test clears it, and it requires the regulator to be informed within 48 hours?

items.explanation: Holding the price and investing in the network is right only if buyers value the network more than price and the network is a real advantage worth building. The correct option establishes both: buyers rank service above price, and the firm's 200 centres are the largest network. The other options support only the price decision, or cite a future cost change, a subsidy, or the rival's plans, none of which supports investing in the network.
options: Most buyers rank the service network above a lower price, and a 20 percent cut would make every vehicle loss-making.
The rival plans to raise its prices after the festive season, and first-time buyers care only about price.
A cheaper battery supplier will be available next year, and the firm's dealers want bigger discounts.
Most buyers of electric two-wheelers rank the service network and spare parts availability above a lower price, and the firm's 200 service centres are the largest network in the segment.
The government offers a subsidy to buyers of electric two-wheelers, and the rival has only 40 service centres.
items.passage: A maker of electric two-wheelers has seen its sales fall by 30 percent in six months after a new rival launched a similar vehicle at 25 percent below its price. The rival vehicle has a shorter range and a smaller service network, but its low price has attracted first-time buyers who have never owned an electric vehicle. The firm's own vehicle has a longer range, a network of 200 service centres, and a five-year battery warranty, while the rival offers only a two-year warranty and 40 service centres. The sales head wants to cut the price by 20 percent to match the rival, arguing that first-time buyers care only about price and that market share is being lost every week. The finance head warns that a 20 percent cut would make every vehicle loss-making, and that the firm would run out of cash within a year at that price. The product head argues that the firm should instead improve its financing offers and its service network, and let the rival's buyers discover the cost of poor service. The chief executive must decide before the festive season, when two-wheeler sales double and the rival is planning a large advertising campaign. The festive season starts in eight weeks, when two-wheeler sales double and the rival is planning a large advertising campaign. The firm's dealers have asked for bigger discounts to match the rival's price, and two dealers have said they will switch to the rival if the firm does not act. The finance head has calculated that a 20 percent price cut would make every vehicle loss-making and that the firm would run out of cash within a year. The product head has proposed better financing offers and a stronger service network instead.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support holding the price AND investing further in the service network rather than cutting the price by 20 percent?
items.stream_verdict: REBUILD: Single-step matching: option C restates the passage's own point that buyers rank service network and spares above price.

items.explanation: Holding the price is justified by three legs: a cut would make every vehicle loss-making and exhaust the firm's cash (A), the firm's real advantages are range, service and warranty (B), and there is a workable alternative in financing and service (E). (C) describes the rival's appeal, and (D) describes the sales fall, which argues for acting rather than for holding the price. Five facts have come to light. (A) A 20 percent price cut would make every vehicle loss-making, and the firm would run out of cash within a year at that price. (B) The firm's vehicle has a longer range, a network of 200 service centres, and a five-year battery warranty, while the rival offers a two-year warranty and 40 service centres. (C) The rival vehicle has a shorter range and a smaller service network, but its low price has attracted first-time buyers. (D) Sales have fallen by 30 percent in six months, and dealers have asked for bigger discounts. (E) The product head has proposed better financing offers and a stronger service network instead of a price cut. Which combination of three facts MOST helps the chief executive hold the price and compete on range, service and warranty instead?

items.explanation: The rule attacks both causes: a price cut that destroys the firm, and no tested alternative to cutting. Cutting whenever a rival launches repeats the loss, closing service centres destroys the advantage, and shortening the warranty gives away the firm's best argument.
options: The firm will cut its price by 20 percent whenever a rival launches, whatever the cost, so that market share never falls
The firm will close its service centres, so that its costs match the rival's
The firm will shorten its battery warranty to two years, so that it matches the rival's offer

The board now asks for a rule that will stop a rival's price cut from ever again forcing the firm to choose between losing sales and losing money. Which rule best prevents a recurrence?

The other options support only the first part, or cite the mine's benefits, or restate the company's offer without showing its gap.

The mine's water use has already lowered the water table and village wells are running dry, and the company's offered borewell would take a year to dig while its water tankers cover only six months.
The mine pays a large share of the district's tax revenue, and its mining licence is due for renewal next year.
The company has offered to dig a new borewell for the village, and the village council has threatened a protest.
The farmers' crops have failed for two seasons, and the mine is the largest employer in the district.
items.passage: A mining company operates an iron ore mine that employs 400 people and pays a large share of the district's tax revenue. The mine uses large amounts of groundwater, and the water table in the surrounding villages has fallen sharply in the last three years. Village wells are running dry, farmers say their crops have failed for two seasons, and women now walk four kilometres to fetch water. The company argues that it holds a valid mining licence, that it pays compensation to affected families, and that closing or limiting the mine would leave 400 families without income. The village council has asked the district officer to limit the mine's water use and to require the company to supply water to the villages until the water table recovers. The company offers to dig a new borewell for the village and to pay for water tankers for six months, but refuses to limit its own water use, arguing that its production targets depend on it. The district officer must decide before the summer, when the water shortage will be at its worst and the village council has threatened a protest that would block the road to the mine. The summer starts in two months, when the water shortage will be at its worst and the village council has threatened a protest that would block the road to the mine. The farmers say their crops have failed for two seasons and women now walk four kilometres to fetch water. The company has offered to dig a new borewell and to pay for water tankers for six months, but it refuses to limit its own water use. The district officer must decide before the summer, and the mine's licence is due for renewal next year.

items.explanation: If the chief executive has already told the board about the illness and asked for a succession plan, the information is not a secret the human resources head must protect, which supports discussing it openly with the board. The illness being private is a reason for care, not a reason to hide a succession risk. A rival learning of it is a risk to manage. The head's friendship with the chief executive is a conflict, not a justification. The board meeting being next week is a deadline, not evidence.
options: The illness is a private medical matter and the chief executive has asked for confidentiality
A rival firm could use the news to poach the company's clients
The human resources head is a close friend of the chief executive
The chief executive has already told the board about the illness and asked the head to prepare a succession plan
The board meeting is next week and the succession item is on the agenda
items.passage: The human resources head of a listed company has learned from the chief executive's doctor, who is a personal friend, that the chief executive has a serious illness and may need to step down within six months. The chief executive has asked the human resources head to keep the information completely confidential, saying the chief executive will tell the board when the time is right. The human resources head knows that the board is about to approve a three-year strategy that depends on the chief executive leading it, that investors have been told the chief executive will stay for at least three years, and that the company has no succession plan. The head also knows that revealing the illness without the chief executive's consent would breach a personal confidence and could be seen as a betrayal. The head must decide whether to tell the board chair in confidence, to wait for the chief executive to disclose, or to raise the absence of a succession plan without mentioning the illness. The board meeting is in two weeks, and the strategy vote cannot be delayed without a public explanation. The board meeting is in two weeks and the strategy vote cannot be delayed without a public explanation to investors. The company has no succession plan and no deputy chief executive who could step in if the chief executive had to leave suddenly. Investors have been told the chief executive will stay for at least three years, and the three-year strategy depends on the chief executive leading it. The human resources head learned the information from the chief executive's doctor, who is a personal friend, and the chief executive has asked for complete confidentiality.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support telling the board chair in confidence?

items.explanation: Telling the chair is justified by three legs: the strategy depends on one person for three years (A), investors have been told that person will stay (B), and there is no succession plan if that person leaves suddenly (D). (C) argues for waiting, and (E) is about how the head learned the information, which is a reason for care rather than a reason to raise the succession plan. Every distractor triple contains two right facts and one that does not support telling the chair.
options: (A), (C) and (E)

items.question: A week later, the board meeting is in two weeks and the strategy vote cannot be delayed without a public explanation. The company has no deputy chief executive who could step in. Five facts have come to light. (A) The board is about to approve a three-year strategy that depends on the chief executive leading it. (B) Investors have been told the chief executive will stay for at least three years. (C) The chief executive has asked the human resources head to keep the illness completely confidential, saying the chief executive will tell the board when the time is right. (D) The company has no succession plan and no deputy chief executive who could step in if the chief executive had to leave suddenly. Which combination of three facts MOST helps the human resources head tell the board chair in confidence that a succession plan is urgently needed, without disclosing the illness?

items.explanation: The rule must do two things: name a successor for every role a strategy depends on, and review the succession plan every year whether or not anyone is ill. Only the third option does both. The last option names successors but reviews the plan only after someone falls ill, so it fails the second condition. Asking the chief executive to stay does not create a plan, writing plans only after illness repeats the problem, and keeping health information secret hides the risk from the board.
options: The chief executive will be asked to stay for at least three years, whatever their health
Succession plans will be written only after a chief executive falls ill
Every three-year strategy must name a successor for each role it depends on, and the board will review the succession plan every year, whether or not anyone is ill
The human resources head will be told to keep all health information secret, even from the board chair

items.question: The board chair has been told in confidence and a succession plan is now in place. The board now asks for a rule that will stop the company from ever again depending on one person with no succession plan. Which rule does BOTH things: it requires every three-year strategy to name a successor for each role it depends on, and it requires the board to review the succession plan every year, whether or not anyone is ill?

items.explanation: Three experienced nurses resigning because of the surgeon's shouting shows the behaviour is already costing the hospital skilled staff, which is a concrete reason to act now. The surgeon's skill and the long waiting list explain why the director hesitates, but they do not make the behaviour acceptable. A rival offer is a risk, not evidence. A single apology last year does not undo a continuing pattern.
options: The surgeon is the most skilled in the hospital for complex operations
Three experienced nurses have resigned in the last six months, citing the surgeon's shouting and public humiliation of staff in the operating theatre
The waiting list for the surgeon's operations is six months long
A rival hospital has offered the surgeon a higher salary
The surgeon apologised once after a complaint last year
items.passage: A large hospital has a senior surgeon who performs complex operations that no other surgeon in the hospital can do, and whose patients have the best outcomes in the region. The same surgeon routinely shouts at nurses and junior doctors in the operating theatre, has thrown instruments on the floor twice, and has made two junior doctors cry in front of patients. Three experienced nurses have resigned in the last six months, citing the surgeon's behaviour, and the nursing head warns that more will leave. The hospital director fears that disciplining the surgeon could lead to the surgeon's resignation, which would leave complex cases with no one to treat them and would damage the hospital's reputation. The hospital has a written code of conduct that applies to all staff, and the medical council can suspend a doctor for repeated unprofessional behaviour. The director must decide before the next appraisal, when the surgeon expects the highest rating and a promotion to head of department, a role that would give the surgeon authority over the nurses who complained. The hospital director must decide before the next appraisal, when the surgeon expects the highest rating and a promotion to head of department. The nursing head has warned that more nurses will leave if the behaviour continues, and the hospital already struggles to recruit experienced theatre nurses. The medical council can suspend a doctor for repeated unprofessional behaviour, and the hospital's code of conduct applies to all staff regardless of skill. The surgeon's patients have the best outcomes in the region, which is why the director fears losing the surgeon.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support acting against the surgeon's behaviour now?

items.explanation: Refusing the promotion is justified by three legs: the behaviour is documented and repeated (B), the code applies to all staff and the medical council can suspend for it (C), and nurses are already leaving because of it (E). (A) argues for keeping the surgeon, and (D) describes the promotion at stake rather than a reason to refuse it. Every distractor triple contains two right facts and one that points the wrong way.
options: (B), (C) and (E)

items.explanation: The phased transition needs two things: proof that the system's errors matter, and proof that the analysts hold knowledge the system lacks. Only the fourth option gives both: two bad loans already caused by the system's errors, and client knowledge the system does not have. The last option gives the errors but removes the need for the analysts, since their knowledge has been copied. The system's speed and cost argue for immediate dismissal, the chief executive's wish is the proposal being opposed, and the licence renewal is irrelevant to the transition.
options: The system is faster and cheaper than the analysts, and the savings will fund growth
The chief executive wants to dismiss all 80 analysts at once and rely on the system
The system licence must be renewed before the next quarterly results

The system's errors on complex cases have already caused two bad loans, and the analysts hold knowledge about long-standing clients that the system does not have, so the firm needs their judgement while the system is checked

The system's errors on complex cases have already caused two bad loans, but the analysts' knowledge about long-standing clients has already been copied into the system, so their judgement is no longer needed
items.passage: A financial services firm has bought an automated system that can do the routine work of 80 analysts, who check loan applications and prepare credit reports.
